group.passage:
Humans might begin to pick up languages earlier than most people think. Research findings show that fetuses can hear towards the end of pregnancy. In addition, newborns can recognize their mother tongue and even prefer their mothers’ voices as well as the languages they spoke during pregnancy, which further implies the possible influence of prenatal exposure.
Benedetta Mariani, a Ph.D. student at the Padova Neuroscience Center, and her colleagues delved into this phenomenon by monitoring the brain waves of newborns who had been exposed to their mothers’ native language before birth. The researchers measured the brain activity of 33 babies born to native French-speaking mothers between one and five days after birth. With electroencephalography (EEG), a test measuring electrical activity in the brain, brain waves were detected in areas responsible for processing speech and sound units, such as syllables and phonemes.
During the experiment, the fairy tale, “Goldilocks and the Three Bears” was played in French, Spanish, and English to sleeping babies. Different language versions were set in various orders but all started and ended with three-minute silence. Meanwhile, EEG caps were placed on the babies’ heads to monitor the brain waves in the regions associated with auditory and speech perceptions. It was found that when the babies listened to the French audio, a spike which was linked to speech perception and processing emerged, and that the signals were reduced when other languages were played. The research results can to some extent support the idea that prenatal language exposure plays a role.
Do babies who miss out on prenatal language priming, such as international adoptees or deaf infants, suffer developmentally later in life? Researchers indicate that prenatal language experience scaffolds, or supports, language development, but doesn’t determine or guarantee development outcomes. Further studies need to be conducted to investigate how long the influence of prenatal exposure can last.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be considered an example of prenatal exposure?

options.A: Mothers lie next to their babies and put them to bed.
options.B: Fathers take responsibility for disciplining their children.
options.C: Parents chit-chat to the belly of the mother-to-be from time to time.
options.D: Kindergartens and primary schools offer an all-English environment.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Failing to gain early language input hinders deaf children’s language development.
options.B: The study suggests that fetuses have started to perceive the basic elements of human speech.
options.C: In the experiment, only when the French version was the first to be played did babies respond.
options.D: In the research, EEG was placed on the babies’ heads to keep out any disturbance from outside.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the experiment?

options.A: To understand the role of prenatal exposure in language processing.
options.B: To find out if babies can learn multiple languages simultaneously.
options.C: To determine which language is the easiest for babies to learn.
options.D: To see if babies prefer stories narrated by their mothers.

questions.stem: Which question might future studies deal with based on Benedetta Mariani’s findings?

options.A: Do physically healthy children perform linguistically better than the disabled ones?
options.B: What can the international adoptees do to make up for the missed prenatal language input?
options.C: Which part of the brain is responsible for the auditory and speech perception of infants?
options.D: Does prenatal exposure continue to influence a newborn baby’s language development?
